# Overview

Your group has just been hired as the data science team for a city **Environmental Health Bureau**. The bureau's director is a **physician**, not a statistician or data scientist, and she decides when to issue **air-pollution health advisories**. She has asked you:

1. **Which weather conditions, seasons, and locations go along with higher fine-particle air pollution (PM~2.5~)?** (a *number* — µg/m³)
2. **On which days is the air most likely to be "unhealthy"?** (a *yes/no* outcome)

You have four years of **hourly** air-quality and weather readings from 12 monitoring stations in Beijing (March 2013 to February 2017). You will take this file through the full data science pipeline — wrangling, missing data, summary statistics, visualization, and modeling with both **traditional regression** and **machine learning** — and then **explain your findings to the director in plain language.**

<div class="keyidea">
**You are writing for the director.** She decides when to warn the public, but will not read R code. Every justification, interpretation, and conclusion in this report must be written so that **an intelligent person with no statistics background** can follow it. Points throughout are for your *reasoning and communication*, not just correct code.
</div>

## Why PM~2.5~ matters

PM~2.5~ are airborne particles 2.5 micrometers or smaller — small enough to reach deep into the lungs and the bloodstream. Short-term exposure is linked to asthma attacks, hospital admissions for heart and lung disease, and excess deaths. In this project, an **"unhealthy day"** is a day whose **24-hour average PM~2.5~ is above 75 µg/m³**, China's national standard (GB 3095-2012, Grade II) during the study period. For comparison, the current U.S. EPA 24-hour standard is 35 µg/m³ and the World Health Organization guideline is 15 µg/m³.

# The Data

`beijing_air_quality.csv` has **one row per station per hour** (about 420,000 rows). Keep it in the same folder as this `.Rmd`.

| Variable | Description | Units |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `No` | Row number within each station's original file | — |
| `year`, `month`, `day`, `hour` | Date and hour of the reading (`hour` runs 0–23) | — |
| `PM2.5` | Fine particulate matter concentration | µg/m³ |
| `PM10` | Coarse + fine particulate matter concentration | µg/m³ |
| `SO2` | Sulfur dioxide concentration | µg/m³ |
| `NO2` | Nitrogen dioxide concentration | µg/m³ |
| `CO` | Carbon monoxide concentration | µg/m³ |
| `O3` | Ozone concentration | µg/m³ |
| `TEMP` | Air temperature | °C |
| `PRES` | Atmospheric pressure | hPa |
| `DEWP` | Dew point temperature (higher = more moisture in the air) | °C |
| `RAIN` | Precipitation in that hour | mm |
| `wd` | Wind direction (16 compass points, e.g., `N`, `NNE`, `NE`, …) | — |
| `WSPM` | Wind speed | m/s |
| `station` | Name of the monitoring station (12 stations) | — |

**Source / citation.** Zhang S, Guo B, Dong A, He J, Xu Z, Chen SX. Cautionary tales on air-quality improvement in Beijing. *Proceedings of the Royal Society A.* 2017;473:20170457. [Full text](https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rspa.2017.0457) · [UCI data page](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/501/beijing+multi+site+air+quality+data)

<div class="tip">
**Keep in mind:** these are observational data, so your models describe **associations, not causes**. You are also modeling **air pollution itself**, not a health outcome — linking pollution to illness would be the real-world next step.
</div>

### Question 2.2 — Build the daily dataset (8 points)

a) Build `air_daily` with **one row per station per day**, working through the three steps below.

**Step 1 — Daily averages.** From the hourly data, `group_by(station, date, season)` and then use `summarize()` to create:

| New variable | What it should contain | Function |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `pm25_hours` | number of hours that day with a non-missing PM~2.5~ | `sum(!is.na(pm25))` |
| `pm25` | daily **average** PM~2.5~ | `mean(..., na.rm = TRUE)` |
| `temp`, `dewp`, `wspm` | daily averages of `TEMP`, `DEWP`, `WSPM` | `mean(..., na.rm = TRUE)` |
| `rain` | daily **total** rainfall | `sum(..., na.rm = TRUE)` |

Add `.groups = "drop"`. Save as `daily_means`.

**Step 2 — Most common wind direction each day.** Create a new data frame called `daily_wind`. 
From the hourly data: 

* Remove missing values for `wind_dir` using `filter()`.
* Use `count(station, date, wind_dir)` to tally how many hours each wind direction occurred, separately for every station on every day. This collapses the 24 hourly rows into at most a few rows per station-day — one per direction that showed up — and adds a new column `n` holding those hour counts.
* Now use `group_by(station, date)` and then `slice_max(n, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)`. Within each station-day group, this code keeps the single row with the largest n — i.e., the direction that blew the most hours that day. Two things to note about the arguments: the `n = 1` is `slice_max`'s own "how many rows to keep" argument (confusingly, it’s unrelated to the count column that also happens to be named `n`); and `with_ties = FALSE` forces exactly one row even on a tie — without it, a day split 12–12 between two directions would return both rows and break the "one row per station-day" guarantee. On a tie it keeps whichever the data lists first, which is arbitrary but harmless here.
* Remove the grouping using `ungroup()`.
* Use the `select` function to keep the only columns needed, `station`, `date`, and `wind_dir`.

**Step 3 — Join and apply a completeness rule.** Create a new data frame called `air_daily`:

* left_join()` `daily_wind` onto `daily_means` by `station` and `date`.
* Use `mutate()` to set `pm25` to `NA` for any station-day with **fewer than 18 valid hours**. Use this code: (`if_else(pm25_hours < 18, NA_real_, pm25)`), and make `wind_dir` a factor. 

b) Report the dimensions of `air_daily`.
c) Report how many station-days have a missing `pm25` after the rule.

<div class="tip">
**Check your work:** `air_daily` should have one row for each of the 12 stations on each of the 1,461 days (≈ 17,532 rows). Far more rows → check your `group_by()`. Far fewer → check your join. `NA_real_` (not plain `NA`) is needed because `if_else()` wants both outcomes to be the same type.
</div>

# Part 3: Managing Missing Data (8 points)

### Question 3.1 (4 points)

```{r q3-1-provided, eval = FALSE}
air_daily %>%
  summarize(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "n_missing") %>%
  mutate(pct_missing = round(100 * n_missing / nrow(air_daily), 2))
```
